title: The Suvarnaprabhasa Sutra — the Sanskrit text
textType: Mahayana sutra in prose and verse
attributionNote: The Sutra of Golden Light, transmitted without an author and expanded as it was copied: in East Asia and Tibet it became a scripture of state protection and of the daily confession, while its dhāraṇī chapters were carried as amulets. GRETIL's e-text follows S. Bagchi's edition (Darbhanga 1967, Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 8) and was input by the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon Input Project.
description: The Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra teaches that the Buddha's teaching endures in the world as a golden light that shines over the realm of the king who protects it: its chapters praise the sutra itself and promise the protection of the four great kings, the goddess Sarasvatī, the nāga kings and the earth goddesses to those who keep it; they set out the confession of sins and the conduct of a Bodhisattva, the story of the earth goddess Dṛḍhā and of the prince Jalavāhāna who gives his body for the sake of a hungry tigress, the healing of the sick by the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, and the great assembly of the Buddhas in the closing chapter.
historicalContext: The sutra was translated into Chinese in the fifth century and was recited in Japan as the Golden Light Sutra whose protection the state invoked against famine and rebellion; its Tibetan translation and the verses of its closing chapter are among the best known of all Buddhist texts.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: all fifteen chapters with their prose and verse, 546 passages, streamed from GRETIL at read time, one chapter at a time. The file prints its title and the first chapter's heading above the opening, and the reader drops them from the text. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
